x: When you have to have it No state requires tenants to carry renters insurance. A landlord can require it in the lease, and many do, especially larger apartment buildings. The lease usually sets a minimum liability limit, often $100,000, and asks you to list the landlord as an "interested party" so they hear if the policy lapses. Why it's worth having anyway The landlord's insurance covers the building, not you. Without your own policy, you pay for these yourself: Your belongings after a fire, theft, smoke or a burst pipe, including things stolen from your car. A hotel and meals if the apartment becomes unlivable after a covered loss (loss of use). Damage you cause, like an overflowing bathtub that ruins the unit below, and injuries to guests (personal liability). It's one of the cheaper policies you can buy, often less than a streaming subscription or two per month. What it doesn't cover Flood and earthquake damage. Each needs its own policy. Your roommate's things, unless they're named on your policy. Pests like bedbugs.

t: Can I get car insurance with a foreign driver's license?
d: Yes, some insurers will cover you, but you'll have fewer choices and pay more. Getting a US state license soon is the single biggest fix.
x: What to expect Fewer insurers: many only quote drivers with a US license. Others accept a foreign or international license, usually at a higher price. New-driver pricing: your years of driving abroad usually don't count, so you may be priced like a beginner until you build a US record. A few insurers accept driving records from some countries, so ask. Credit history: in most states insurers use credit to price car insurance, and a new arrival has none yet. Your license may stop being valid Once you become a resident of a state, most states expect you to get their license within a set time, often somewhere between 10 and 90 days. After that, driving on a foreign license can be illegal, and a crash could become a claims problem. An International Driving Permit is only a translation of your home license, not a license of its own. Check your state's motor vehicle agency for the exact rule, and book the tests early, because appointments can take weeks. What you need to buy Almost every state requires liability insurance before you drive. State minimum limits are low; higher limits protect your savings if you cause a serious crash. If you have a car loan or lease, the lender will also require collision and comprehensive.

d: Extra liability coverage on top of your home and car policies, usually $1 million or more, for when someone sues you for more than those policies pay.
x: How it works Say you cause a crash and the other driver's injuries lead to a $700,000 judgment. Your car policy pays up to its liability limit, say $300,000. Without an umbrella, the other $400,000 can come from your savings and future wages. An umbrella policy pays that part. Insurers require you to keep certain limits on your home and car policies first, for example $300,000 of personal liability. The umbrella starts where they stop. What it usually covers Injuries and property damage you cause to others, at home, in your car and elsewhere. Your legal defense, often on top of the limit. In many policies, claims your other policies don't cover, like libel, slander or false arrest. What it doesn't cover Damage to your own house, car or belongings. Your business activities. That needs a commercial umbrella. Harm you cause on purpose.

t: HMO vs PPO: what's the difference?
d: An HMO covers care only from its own network and often needs a referral to see a specialist. A PPO lets you go outside the network for a higher share of the cost, and usually costs more each month.
x: Side by side HMO: you pick a primary care doctor, who refers you to specialists. Care outside the network isn't covered except in emergencies. Premiums are usually lower. PPO: no referrals needed. Out-of-network care is covered, but you pay more of it, and the out-of-network provider can bill you the difference. Premiums are usually higher. EPO: in between. No referrals, but like an HMO, nothing outside the network except emergencies. How to choose Look up your doctors first. If they're all in the HMO's network and you don't mind referrals, the HMO is usually the cheaper choice. If you want to keep a doctor outside the network, travel a lot within the US, or have family in another state, a PPO can be worth the higher premium. Emergencies are protected either way. Plans must cover emergency care outside the network at in-network cost sharing, and federal law protects you from most surprise bills from out-of-network providers in emergencies and at in-network hospitals.

t: I missed open enrollment. Can I still get health insurance?
d: Only if a life event gives you a special enrollment period, like moving, losing other coverage, marriage or a new baby. Medicaid and CHIP accept people all year.
x: Events that open a special enrollment period Outside open enrollment, you can buy a marketplace plan only during a special enrollment period. You usually have 60 days from the event. Common ones: Losing health coverage, for example when a job ends. Quitting a plan or not paying premiums doesn't count. Moving to a new ZIP code or county, or moving to the US. Getting married, having or adopting a child. Big income changes that make you newly eligible for help with premiums, in some cases. Employer plans have their own window A job-based plan has its own enrollment period, often in the fall. Life events like marriage or losing other coverage also let you join it mid-year, but usually only within 30 days. If you lose a job-based plan, you can often keep it for a while through COBRA, at the full price. Be careful with stopgap plans Short-term health plans can be bought any time, but they don't have to cover pre-existing conditions or all the basics a Marketplace plan must cover. Read what's excluded before relying on one.

t: Does my car insurance cover a rental car?
d: Usually yes, within the US and for personal use: your policy's coverage carries over to the rental. It covers damage to the rental only if you carry collision and comprehensive on your own car.
x: What carries over Liability for injuries and damage you cause to others, up to your limits. Damage to the rental only if you have collision and comprehensive, minus your deductible. The rental company may also charge for the days the car can't be rented and an administrative fee. Many personal policies don't pay those. When you may need the rental company's cover You don't own a car and have no policy, so there's nothing to carry over. You're renting abroad. Most US car policies cover only the US and Canada. You're renting for work. Your employer's policy or a business policy is the one to check. You carry only liability on your own car and don't want to pay for rental damage yourself. The damage waiver sold at the counter isn't insurance: the rental company agrees not to charge you for damage. Many credit cards include rental car coverage, but it often only pays what your own policy doesn't. Check before you travel.

t: What insurance do I need as a freelancer?
d: Health coverage first, since no employer provides it. After that, it depends on the work: professional liability if you give advice or build things for clients, general liability if you work at client sites, and cover for your equipment.
x: For you Health insurance from the marketplace or a spouse's plan. Self-employed people can often deduct the premiums. Disability insurance, because no employer plan replaces your income if you can't work. For the work Professional liability (E&O) if a client could blame your advice, design or code for their losses. Consultants, designers and developers usually need this first. General liability if you work at client sites or meet clients in person. Many client contracts require it and ask for a certificate of insurance. Your equipment: a home or renters policy usually covers business equipment only up to a small amount, often $2,500. A business owner's policy or inland marine cover fills the gap. Your car: a personal car policy may not cover driving that is part of the job, like deliveries. Tell your insurer. An LLC doesn't replace insurance An LLC can keep business debts away from your personal assets, but it usually won't protect you from claims about your own professional mistakes. Workers' compensation usually only becomes required once you hire employees, and the rules vary by state.

t: Is an explanation of benefits a bill?
d: No. An explanation of benefits (EOB) is your health plan's summary of a claim. The bill comes separately from the doctor or hospital, and it should match what the EOB says you owe.
x: How to read one Amount billed: what the provider charged. Allowed amount: what your plan has agreed to pay for that service. In-network providers can't charge you more than this. Plan paid: what the insurer paid. You may owe: your share, from your deductible, copay or coinsurance. What to do with it Keep the EOB until the bill arrives, then compare the two. If the bill asks for more than "you may owe", call the provider's billing office first, then your plan. If the claim was denied, the EOB gives a reason code. You can ask the plan to reconsider through an internal appeal, and if it still says no, ask for an independent external review.

d: No. Standard home and renters policies exclude flood. You need a separate flood policy, and it usually takes 30 days to start.
x: What counts as flood Flood means water rising from outside and covering normally dry land: an overflowing river, storm surge, or heavy rain that pools and pours in. Water from a burst pipe inside the house is not flood, and your home policy covers it. Where to get flood insurance The National Flood Insurance Program sells through regular insurance agents. It covers up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. Private flood insurers can offer higher limits and sometimes shorter waiting periods. Renters can buy contents-only flood cover. NFIP coverage usually starts 30 days after you buy it, so buying when a storm is forecast is too late. Do you need it outside a flood zone? Lenders require flood insurance only in high-risk flood zones, but many flood claims come from lower-risk areas. Federal disaster aid, when it's available, is limited and often a loan you have to pay back.

t: Is health insurance mandatory in the US?
d: Not under federal law: there has been no federal penalty since 2019. But a few states require it, and some visas do too.
x: States that require coverage California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Washington, D.C. charge a tax penalty if you go without coverage, unless you qualify for an exemption. Vermont requires coverage but has no penalty. Rules can change, so check your state's tax agency or insurance marketplace. Visas with their own rules Some visas set minimum coverage, notably J-1 exchange visitors and their dependents. Universities often require international students to carry the school plan or an equivalent. Why go insured even where it's optional US medical care is expensive: a hospital stay can cost tens of thousands of dollars. A plan's out-of-pocket maximum caps what you pay in a year for covered care.

t: Does renters insurance cover things stolen outside my home?
d: Usually yes. A standard renters policy covers your belongings almost anywhere, so a laptop stolen from a café, a bike taken from a rack or things stolen from your car are covered, minus your deductible.
x: What is covered away from home The personal property part of a standard renters policy follows your things, not just your apartment. Theft is a covered cause wherever it happens, including: Items stolen from your car. Car insurance doesn't cover these; renters insurance does. A bike stolen from a rack or a bag taken while you travel. Things you keep in a storage unit, though some policies pay less for property kept somewhere you don't live. Where it falls short Your deductible comes off first, so a $300 bike with a $500 deductible pays nothing. Jewelry, watches and some other valuables have a low theft limit, often around $1,500 in total, unless you list them as scheduled personal property. Simply losing something isn't theft and usually isn't covered. Damage to the car itself, like a broken window, is a car insurance claim under comprehensive. Report the theft to the police and keep the report number. Insurers usually ask for it.

t: Do I need dental and vision insurance in the US?
d: It's optional for adults. Most health plans don't cover adult dental care or glasses, so they're sold as separate, fairly small plans. Children's dental and vision are a standard benefit.
x: Why it's separate Marketplace and most job-based health plans must cover dental and vision care for children, but not for adults. Adults usually get it through a separate dental plan and a separate vision plan, either from an employer or bought alongside a marketplace health plan. What these plans usually pay Dental: checkups and cleanings are often fully covered. Fillings and bigger work like crowns are partly covered, sometimes only after a waiting period, and most plans cap what they pay in a year, often at $1,000 to $2,000. Vision: a yearly eye exam plus an allowance toward glasses or contact lenses. Is it worth it? If your employer offers it, it's usually cheap and worth taking. On your own, compare a year of premiums with what you expect to spend: dental plans help most with regular care, less with big unexpected work because of the yearly cap. Eye injuries and eye diseases are usually covered by your health plan, not a vision plan. Dental "discount plans" are not insurance. They get you a lower price from certain dentists but pay nothing themselves.

t: What is a certificate of insurance?
d: A one-page summary that proves your business has insurance: which policies, with which insurer, the limits and the dates. Clients and landlords often ask for one before you start work.
x: What it shows A certificate of insurance lists your insurer, policy numbers, policy dates and limits for coverages like general liability, car, workers' compensation and professional liability. In the US it's usually on a standard form called ACORD 25. You get it from your insurance agent, broker or insurer's website, usually free and within a day. A certificate isn't coverage by itself It only describes your policy. If a client wants to be covered by your policy for claims from your work, the policy needs an additional insured endorsement naming them. Writing their name on the certificate alone doesn't do that. Before you send one, check that the limits match what the contract asks for and that the dates cover the whole job.

t: A pipe bursts and floods my kitchen.
d: Sudden water from inside the house is usually covered.
x: Home, condo and renters policies cover sudden, accidental water damage from plumbing. The broken pipe itself usually isn't replaced. A frozen pipe in a house left unheated can be excluded. water leak plumbing frozen

d: Water from outside isn't covered by a home policy.
x: Home policies exclude surface water and groundwater seeping in. A flood policy pays only if the event meets the official flood definition, and even then covers little in a basement. If a sump pump overflowed, a water backup coverage endorsement may pay. Rain coming in through a storm-damaged roof or wall is covered by your home policy. water storm rain flooding

t: Sewage backs up through a floor drain.
d: Only if you added water backup coverage.
x: Standard policies exclude water that backs up through sewers or drains, or overflows a sump pump. A water backup coverage endorsement adds it, usually for a small extra premium. water sump pump drain

t: A slow leak under the sink caused mold over several months.
d: Slow, ongoing leaks and the mold they cause are excluded.
x: Policies cover sudden damage, not damage that builds up over time. Insurers expect you to notice and fix slow leaks. Some policies cover a little mold removal when it results from a covered sudden leak. mold water maintenance

t: A tree falls on my house in a storm.
d: Damage to the house and removing the tree from it are covered.
x: Your own policy pays, whoever owned the tree. If a neighbor ignored a visibly dead tree, your insurer may try to recover from them. A tree that falls without hitting anything is usually only removed up to a small amount. wind storm tree

d: Wear and tear isn't covered.
x: If the roof leaks because of age, the insurer treats it as maintenance. Storm damage to a roof is covered, though some policies pay only the depreciated value for older roofs. roof maintenance leak

d: Hail is covered, minus your deductible.
x: In hail-prone states, there may be a separate wind and hail deductible, often a percentage of your dwelling limit. Some policies pay older roofs at actual cash value. storm roof wind

d: Only up to a low limit, unless it's listed on your policy.
x: Jewelry theft is usually capped at around $1,500 in total. If the ring is listed as scheduled personal property, it's covered for its appraised value. jewelry theft valuables

t: I lost my ring down the drain.
d: Simply losing something isn't a covered cause, unless it's scheduled.
x: Losing an item isn't one of the named perils. Items listed as scheduled personal property are usually covered for loss too. jewelry lost valuables

t: A power surge fries my TV.
d: It depends on what caused the surge.
x: Lightning damage is covered. A surge from the power company is a named peril, but the standard wording excludes damage to electronic parts, so many TVs and computers aren't covered. Some insurers add surge coverage. electronics lightning electric

d: Earthquakes are excluded; you need a separate policy.
x: Ground movement is excluded from standard home policies. An earthquake policy or add-on covers it, with a high percentage deductible. Fire caused by an earthquake is covered by the home policy. quake foundation

t: Wildfire smoke damages my home and belongings.
d: Fire and smoke are covered causes.
x: Fire and smoke are among the most basic covered perils. Extra living costs are covered if you have to leave, including when authorities order an evacuation because a covered cause like fire damaged nearby property, usually for up to two weeks. fire smoke evacuation

d: Pests are excluded.
x: Damage from termites, rodents and other pests is treated as a maintenance issue. pests insects

d: Personal liability usually covers it.
x: The liability part of your home or renters policy pays for the neighbor's injuries and your defense. Some insurers exclude certain breeds or dogs with a bite history, so check. pet animal liability injury

t: A guest slips on my steps and gets hurt.
d: Medical payments and liability cover this.
x: Medical payments to others pays small bills whoever was at fault. If the guest sues, personal liability pays your defense and damages up to the limit. injury liability slip

t: My work laptop is stolen from my home.
d: Not if it belongs to your employer; limited if it's your business's.
x: Your employer's property is for your employer's insurance. Your own business property is covered only up to a small limit, often $2,500 at home. theft business computer remote work

t: My bathtub overflows and damages the apartment below.
d: Your renters liability covers the neighbor's damage.
x: If you're responsible, the liability part of your renters policy pays for the damage to the other unit. Damage to the unit you rent is usually covered only if caused by fire, smoke or explosion. water neighbor liability

t: A fire in another unit ruins my things with smoke.
d: Your renters policy covers your belongings.
x: Smoke and fire are covered causes. The landlord's policy won't replace your things. fire smoke apartment

d: Pests aren't covered.
x: Neither the treatment nor the ruined bedding is covered. Depending on your state and lease, the landlord may be responsible for treatment. pests insects

t: My roommate's laptop is stolen from our apartment.
d: Not on your policy, unless they're named on it.
x: Renters policies cover you and relatives living with you. A roommate needs their own policy or to be added by name. theft roommate

d: Covered by comprehensive, if you carry it.
x: Animal strikes are comprehensive claims. If you swerve and hit a tree instead, that's collision. animal crash

t: I cause a crash. Who pays for my car?
d: Only your collision coverage pays for your own car.
x: Your liability coverage pays for the other driver's car and injuries. Your car is covered only if you carry collision, minus the deductible. accident collision fault

d: Covered if you have uninsured motorist coverage.
x: Uninsured motorist coverage pays your injuries, and in some states your car. Otherwise, collision and your health insurance may pay. accident hit and run

t: A friend borrows my car and crashes.
d: Usually yes: insurance follows the car.
x: Your policy generally covers people driving with your permission. It pays first, and the claim can raise your premium. Regular drivers in your household need to be listed. borrow driver

t: My bag is stolen from my car.
d: Your home or renters policy covers it, not car insurance.
x: Belongings are covered by home or renters insurance wherever they are. Damage to the car, like a broken window, goes to comprehensive. theft break-in

t: My car is flooded in a storm.
d: Comprehensive covers flood damage to cars.
x: Flood insurance doesn't cover cars, but comprehensive on your auto policy does. water storm flood

t: I crash while driving for a delivery or rideshare app.
d: Personal policies usually exclude it.
x: The app company's insurance covers some periods of a trip. A rideshare endorsement on your policy fills the gap. uber lyft doordash gig

t: I get sick before my trip and can't go.
d: Covered by trip cancellation, with a doctor's note.
x: Your own illness, or a close family member's, is a standard covered reason. Conditions you already had may be excluded unless you got a pre-existing condition waiver. cancel illness

d: Travel delay pays meals and a hotel after a waiting period.
x: Usually after 6 to 12 hours, up to a daily limit, for covered causes like weather or mechanical problems. Many credit cards include this if you paid with the card. flight airline delay

t: I don't want to go anymore.
d: Only "cancel for any reason" covers this, partly.
x: Standard policies only refund cancellations for listed reasons. Cancel for any reason refunds 50 to 75% and must be bought early. cancel cfar

d: The airline owes you a refund; insurance may cover the rest.
x: On flights to, from or within the US, airlines must refund cancelled flights in cash if you don't accept a new flight. Travel insurance can cover other prepaid costs, like hotels, if the cause is a covered reason. flight refund

d: The airline pays first; insurance can top up.
x: Airlines owe compensation up to a set limit. Travel insurance pays for essentials while a bag is delayed and can cover losses above what the airline pays, often with caps on electronics and jewelry. baggage bag airline

t: I end up in hospital abroad.
d: Travel medical covers it; your US health plan may not.
x: Many US health plans pay little outside the US, and Medicare usually pays nothing. Travel medical insurance covers emergency care and evacuation up to its limits. medical illness injury abroad

t: I go to an emergency room outside my network.
d: Emergencies are covered at in-network prices.
x: Plans must cover emergency care at in-network cost-sharing, and federal law protects you from most surprise out-of-network bills for emergencies. emergency network hospital surprise bill

t: I see a specialist without a referral on an HMO.
d: HMOs usually require a referral first.
x: Without a referral from your primary care doctor, an HMO may deny the claim. PPOs don't require referrals. doctor referral

t: I have a condition I was treated for before I came to the US.
d: ACA health plans can't exclude it.
x: Marketplace and employer plans can't refuse you or charge more because of a pre-existing condition. Short-term and travel medical plans can. pre-existing expat chronic

d: Adult dental care needs a separate dental plan.
x: Most medical plans don't include adult dental care. Dental plans usually cover fillings partly. dentist teeth

t: A customer slips in my shop.
d: General liability covers customer injuries.
x: The customer's medical bills and any claim, plus your defense, are covered by general liability or the liability part of a BOP. injury slip and fall customer

t: An employee gets hurt at work.
d: Workers' comp covers it, not general liability.
x: Workers' compensation pays medical bills and part of lost wages, regardless of fault. General liability excludes employee injuries. employee injury workplace

t: A client says my advice cost them money.
d: Professional liability covers this; general liability doesn't.
x: Financial harm from your work or advice is covered by professional liability (E&O). General liability only covers physical injury and property damage. consultant mistake negligence

t: We wired money to a scammer after a fake invoice.
d: Only with social engineering fraud coverage.
x: Many cyber and crime policies exclude voluntary transfers unless you added social engineering coverage, often with a low limit. fraud email wire

t: We had to close by government order, with no damage.
d: Business income needs physical damage.
x: Business income coverage is triggered by direct physical loss to property. Closures without damage, such as most pandemic closures, weren't covered. closure pandemic interruption

t: My tools are stolen from my work van.
d: Covered by an equipment (inland marine) policy.
x: Commercial auto covers the van, not what's in it. A contractor's equipment policy covers the tools, often only if the van was locked. theft contractor equipment

d: Fire, wind, theft, water and the other named perils, with examples.
x: Fire or lightning Damage from flames, heat and smoke from a fire, and from lightning strikes. Windstorm or hail Wind, including hurricanes and tornadoes, and hail. Explosion A sudden burst, like a gas leak igniting. Riot or civil commotion Damage by a crowd during a riot or violent disturbance. Aircraft Anything from an aircraft hitting your property, including parts falling off. Vehicles A car or truck hitting your house or belongings. Smoke Sudden, accidental smoke damage, such as from a furnace malfunction or a nearby fire. Vandalism or malicious mischief Damage someone causes on purpose. Theft Things stolen, from your home or elsewhere, and damage done during a break-in. Falling objects Something falling onto the house or your belongings. Weight of ice, snow or sleet Damage when heavy ice or snow makes part of the house give way. Accidental discharge or overflow of water or steam Water that escapes suddenly from plumbing, heating, air conditioning, a sprinkler system or an appliance. Sudden tearing apart, cracking, burning or bulging A water heater, boiler, heating or air-conditioning system, or fire sprinkler system suddenly breaking apart. Freezing Plumbing, heating or air-conditioning systems, or appliances, freezing and breaking. Sudden damage from artificial electrical current Damage from a power surge or short circuit (not lightning, which is covered under fire). Volcanic eruption Damage from lava, ash, dust and blast from an eruption. Flood Earthquake and earth movement Sewer or drain backup Wear and tear Mold and rot Pests and animals Neglect Intentional damage Power failure away from your home Building code upgrades War and nuclear hazard

d: The price of the policy: what you pay the insurer, monthly or yearly, to be covered.
The part of a covered loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays the rest. A higher deductible usually means a lower premium.
The most the policy will pay. Anything above the limit is on you.
A smaller cap inside a larger limit for a specific kind of item or loss.
The most a policy will pay for all claims added together during the policy period, usually one year.
The most a policy will pay for one incident, no matter how many people or claims come from it.
A cause of loss, like fire, wind, theft or a burst pipe.
A way of writing a policy that covers only the causes of loss it lists. If a cause isn't listed, it isn't covered.
A way of writing a policy that covers every cause of loss except the ones it specifically excludes. Broader than named perils.
x: special form, "all risk"

d: Something the policy says it will not cover, even if it would otherwise fit.
A change added to a standard policy that adds, removes or adjusts coverage. Endorsements override the main policy text.
x: rider

d: The summary page of your policy: who and what is insured, the coverages you bought, their limits, your deductibles, the policy period and the price.
x: dec page

d: Paying what it costs to repair or replace something with new, similar quality, with no deduction for age.
Replacement cost minus depreciation, meaning what the item was worth given its age and wear. Pays less than replacement cost.
x: ACV

d: The loss in value from age and wear. Actual cash value payouts subtract it.
Your request to the insurer to pay for a loss under your policy.
The person who investigates a claim and works out how much the insurer owes. Usually works for the insurer. A "public adjuster" works for you, for a fee.
A licensed person who sells insurance. A "captive" agent sells for one company; an "independent" agent can quote several.
A licensed intermediary who shops policies from many insurers on your behalf. Common for business insurance.
After paying you, your insurer can go after the person who caused the loss to get its money back, and often your deductible too.
The dates the policy is in force, often one year for home and business, six or twelve months for car.
Time between buying a policy and when coverage starts, or before a benefit starts paying.
Your legal responsibility for harm you cause to other people or their property. Liability coverage pays their claims against you and your legal defense.
Physical harm to another person, such as a broken arm. Liability coverage pays for their medical bills, lost wages and pain and suffering if you're responsible.
Damage to someone else's property. In liability coverage it pays when you're responsible, like your car hitting their fence.
Pays to repair or rebuild the house itself and things attached to it, like the roof, walls, built-in appliances and a garage attached to the house.
x: Coverage A

d: Covers buildings on your property that aren't attached to the house, like a detached garage, shed or fence. Usually 10% of the dwelling limit.
x: Coverage B

d: Your belongings: furniture, clothes, electronics, kitchenware. Covered at home and usually anywhere in the world.
x: Coverage C, contents

d: Pays extra living costs, like a hotel and restaurant meals above your normal grocery bill, while your home can't be lived in after a covered loss.
x: Coverage D, additional living expenses

d: Pays a landlord the rent they lose while a rental unit can't be lived in after a covered loss.
Pays if you, your family or your pet injure someone or damage their property, and you're legally responsible. Includes your legal defense.
x: Coverage E

d: Pays small medical bills for a guest hurt on your property, no matter who was at fault. Usually $1,000 to $5,000.
x: Coverage F, med pay

d: Listing a valuable item, like an engagement ring, on your policy for its appraised value. It removes the low sublimit and often covers loss, not just theft.
x: floater

d: An add-on for water that backs up through sewers or drains, or overflows a sump pump. Excluded from standard home policies unless you add it.
A separate, larger deductible for wind or hurricane damage, often a percentage of your dwelling limit rather than a dollar amount.
Pays the extra cost of rebuilding to current building codes after a covered loss. Standard policies include only a small amount.
The federal program, run by FEMA (the US disaster agency), that sells most US flood insurance through regular insurance agents.
x: National Flood Insurance Program

d: An area mapped by FEMA, the US federal disaster agency, by how likely it is to flood. In a high-risk zone, most mortgage lenders must require flood insurance.
Your mortgage lender. It's named on your home policy so claim checks for the house include the lender.
The insurance a condo or homeowners association buys for the building and shared areas. What it covers inside units varies, so owners need to know which kind it is.
A charge an association passes on to each owner when a loss to shared property isn't fully paid by its insurance. Loss assessment coverage pays your share.
Pays to repair your own car after it hits another car or an object, or rolls over, whoever was at fault.
Pays for damage to your car from things other than a crash: theft, hail, flood, fire, falling trees, vandalism, hitting a deer.
x: other than collision

d: Pays for your injuries, and in some states your car, when the at-fault driver has no insurance or too little.
x: UM/UIM

d: Pays your and your passengers' medical bills and some lost wages after a crash, no matter who was at fault. Required in no-fault states.
x: PIP

d: A state where your own insurance pays your injury costs after a crash, up to a limit, regardless of fault. You can sue the other driver only for serious injuries. About a dozen states, including Florida, New York and Michigan.
Liability limits written as three numbers, in thousands: injury per person, injury per accident, property damage per accident.
If your car is totaled, pays the difference between what the car is worth and what you still owe on the loan or lease.
A form your insurer files with the state to prove you carry insurance, often required after a serious violation like a DUI or driving uninsured.
A fixed amount you pay for a specific service, like $30 for a doctor visit.
Your percentage share of costs after you meet your deductible.
The most you'll pay for covered, in-network care in a year. After that the plan pays 100%. Premiums don't count toward it.
The doctors and hospitals that have a contract with your health plan. Going outside it costs more, or isn't covered at all.
A health plan that only covers doctors in its network (except emergencies) and usually needs a referral from your primary doctor to see a specialist. Often cheaper.
A health plan that lets you see specialists without a referral and pays part of out-of-network care. Usually a higher premium.
A health plan like an HMO in that it doesn't pay out of network, but usually doesn't need referrals.
A plan with a higher deductible and lower premium that lets you open a tax-free health savings account (HSA).
x: HDHP

d: A tax-advantaged savings account for medical costs, available only with a qualifying high-deductible plan. The money is yours to keep, even if you change jobs.
x: health savings account

d: An employer account you fund from your paycheck, tax-free, for medical costs. Unused money is generally lost at year-end, unless your employer offers a small carryover or grace period.
x: flexible spending account

d: The yearly window when you can sign up for or change health insurance. For HealthCare.gov it usually runs from November 1 to January 15.
A window, usually 60 days, to get health coverage outside open enrollment after a life event like moving to the US, losing job coverage, marriage or a baby.
The government-run place to compare and buy individual health plans. Depending on income you may get help paying the premium. Some states run their own site.
x: exchange, HealthCare.gov

d: A federal rule that lets you keep your employer health plan, usually for up to 18 months, after leaving the job. You pay the full premium plus up to 2%, which is often expensive. It applies to employers with 20 or more employees.
A statement from your health plan showing what a provider billed, what the plan paid, and what you owe. It is not a bill.
x: EOB

d: Approval your health plan requires before some treatments, scans or drugs, or it may not pay.
The person or people who receive the money from a life insurance policy.
Life insurance for a set number of years, like 20 or 30. Pays only if you die in that time. Much cheaper than permanent insurance.
Life insurance meant to last your whole life that also builds a cash value. Much more expensive than term for the same payout.
x: whole life, universal life

d: How long you must be unable to work before disability insurance starts paying, like 90 days.
A travel insurance upgrade that refunds part of your trip cost, usually 50 to 75%, if you cancel for a reason the standard policy doesn't list. It must be bought soon after your first trip payment.
x: CFAR

d: A health problem you had before the coverage started. Travel insurance often excludes it unless you get a waiver by buying early. ACA health plans can't exclude it.
In travel insurance, one of the specific reasons listed in the policy that allow a refund, like your illness or a hurricane at your destination.
Extra liability coverage that starts where your home and car liability limits run out, usually in $1 million steps.
A package for small businesses that combines property insurance, general liability and business income coverage, usually cheaper than buying them separately.
x: BOP

d: Covers a business when it's blamed for injuring someone, damaging their property, or harming them through advertising.
x: CGL, general liability

d: The part of general liability that covers harm caused by something you sold or work you finished, after it left your hands.
Covers incidents that happen during the policy period, even if the claim comes years later. Most general liability works this way.
Covers claims made while the policy is active, for incidents after its retroactive date. Common for professional, cyber and management liability. If you cancel, you may need "tail" coverage.
An add-on to a claims-made policy that lets you report claims after the policy ends, for work done while it was active.
x: extended reporting period

d: Pays the income a business loses, and ongoing bills like rent and payroll, while it's closed after covered physical damage.
x: business interruption

d: Pays the extra costs of keeping a business running after covered damage, like renting a temporary space.
Pays medical bills and part of lost wages for employees hurt or made ill by their job, regardless of fault. In return, employees generally can't sue the employer.
The second part of a workers' comp policy. Covers lawsuits related to work injuries that fall outside workers' comp, like a spouse suing for loss of companionship.
Someone else added to your policy so it also protects them for claims arising from your work. Clients and landlords often require it.
A one-page summary proving a business has insurance, often requested by clients and landlords. It doesn't change the coverage itself.
x: COI

d: Business liability coverage for when you or employees drive rented or personal cars for work.
x: HNOA

d: Despite the name, insurance for business property that moves around, like a contractor's tools, a photographer's gear, or goods in transit.
A rule in business property policies: if you insure a building for less than a set share of its value, usually 80%, claim payments are cut in proportion.
Covers a business against claims from employees or applicants, like wrongful firing, discrimination or harassment.
x: EPLI

d: Covers the people running a company or nonprofit, and often the organization, against claims about their management decisions.
x: D&O

d: Covers claims that your professional advice or service was wrong, late or negligent and cost a client money.
x: errors and omissions, E&O, malpractice

d: Not insurance for you: a guarantee to your client or the state that you'll do what you promised. If the bond pays out, you must repay the bond company.
Premium, deductible, limits, what's covered, and how payouts are calculated.
x: You pay a premium, and share losses through a deductible. The premium is the price of the policy. The deductible is the part of each loss you pay yourself. Limits cap what the insurer pays. A limit is the most the policy pays. Anything above it is yours. Coverage depends on the cause. Policies pay for damage from certain causes, called perils, and exclude others, like flood. New for old, or what it was worth? Replacement cost pays for new. Actual cash value subtracts wear and age. Your losses versus harm you cause others. Some coverage pays for your things and bills. Liability pays for harm you cause other people. Claims leave a record. Claims, even small ones, are logged in a shared industry database and can affect your price. claim denied complaint

d: The declarations page line by line, and how to check if something is covered.
